newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: FOCUS - Tesco deal shows lure of Ireland.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Tesco deal shows lure of Ireland.

text.p: The capture of Ireland's biggest supermarket chain by Britain's top food retailer Tesco underlines the lure of one of Europe's fastest-growing economies for British stores, analysts said on Friday.

Tesco's 630 million pound ($1 billion) takeover of Associated British Food Plc's Quinnsworth and Crazy prices stores marks another British march down the Irish High Street. If the deal, which is subject to EU approval, goes through, it will also give Tesco a firm base in the British province of Northern Ireland, where rival supermarket group Sainsbury is building new stores to cash in on a growing retail market.
The two-pronged attack underscores the attraction of the Irish economy, which is growing at around seven per cent a year, faster than anywhere in the European Union and twice the OECD average.

A mere 75 years after winning independence from British rule, Ireland has again being invaded by its larger neighbour, shopkeepers say. Irish suppliers to Quinnsworth and Crazy Prices were angry at the news of Tesco's coup. They said Tesco's reliance on its own brands would sound the death knell for their produce in the stores of Ireland's major supermarkets.

"In the past five years, the high streets of our major cities have become dominated by UK stores who bring in a large proportion of their products from the UK whilst the considerable profits are repatriated," Brendan Butler, director of Ireland's Small Firms' Association, said.
"The Irish retailer is being squeezed out in a relentless pursuit of a lucrative market by such companies."
Drawn by a "Celtic Tiger" economy and soaring consumer spending, many of the big names in British retailing are at the head of a stampede to set up shop.
Debenhams, Boots and electrical giant Dixons are among British store groups that have recently opened outlets in Dublin, joining established retailers like Marks and Spencer, Next and Body Shop .

For many, getting a toehold in Dublin is the first step in a nationwide assault, designed to take full advantage of the economic boom which has seen Ireland produce an average growth rate of around eight percent over the last two years.
Boots opened its first store in November in Dublin's new Jervis shopping centre and has plans for another four stores, bringing its total investment in Ireland to 7.6 million pounds.

"We are delighted to have the opportunity to invest in Ireland at a time when both the economy and in particular, the health and beauty market, are going through a phenomenal growth phase," Boots' director of business development, Peter Burdon, said.
Dixon says its Dublin store, which opened in December, is just the first step in a 10 million pound, 300-job expansion.
"We plan to open two more Dixons stores next year and a gradual expansion programme will continue as appropriate sites become available," chief executive John Clare said in December.

Clothing and household goods chain Marks and Spencer, in Ireland since 1979, has not been idle. The giant retailer spent 40 million punts ($62.6 million) revamping the old Brown Thomas building on Dublin's busy Grafton Street, turning the 67,000 square feet (6,224 square metres) of retail space into a flagship outlet.
It also completed a three million punt expansion at its city centre store in Cork.
Unlike previous invaders, the latest British arrivals have been welcomed with open arms by the Irish consumer, although the response of Ireland's domestic retailers has been more cautious.
"Retailing is all about consumers and the consumer is the biggest winner with variety and competition," says Declan Martin, economic director of the Dublin Chamber of Commerce.

"The presence of all these people also makes Dublin a more attractive, cosmopolitan European-type city in the sense that there is a far broader choice of shopping and that of course has very positive tourism benefits," he said in an interview.
Others have warned of the threat to sectors such as Irish advertising if the new retailers treat their Irish outlets as if they were merely branches of British chains.
"Companies which enter the Irish market must realise they have a responsibility to use the support services offered by local outfits," warned Ireland's Sunday Tribune.

"It is not good enough merely to ship in all the goods and take the money out, the only contribution to the local economy being the wages and taxes paid." ($ = 0.627 British Pounds) ($ = 0.639 Irish Pounds)
